passages.t: A clay jar and the Valley of Ben-hinnom
passages.happening:
God tells Jeremiah to buy a clay jar from a potter and take some of the elders and the leading priests (verse 1) out to the Valley of Ben-hinnom by the Potsherd Gate (verse 2). There he is to announce a disaster so great that the ears of all who hear of it will ring (verse 3).

The reason: they have abandoned God and made this a foreign place, burning incense to other gods and filling it with the blood of the innocent (verse 4). ‘They have built high places to Baal on which to burn their children in the fire as offerings to Baal’ (verse 5), something God never commanded or mentioned, nor did it enter his mind (verse 5).

So the place will be called the Valley of Slaughter (verse 6). God will bring their plans to nothing, and they will fall by the sword (verse 7). The city will be a desolation that passers-by scoff at (verse 8). Verse 9 then names the worst horror of a siege, what famine drove people to with their own families. These notes name it and do not describe it.
passages.hearers:
The Valley of Ben-hinnom runs along the west and south sides of old Jerusalem. In it lay Topheth, a place where children were sacrificed. The books of Kings record that King Ahaz and later King Manasseh made their sons pass through the fire, and that Josiah defiled Topheth to stop the practice. It had come back.

Child sacrifice was known in the ancient world, especially in times of crisis, as the highest offering to win a god's help. Israel's law forbade it absolutely. God's words that it never entered his mind are as strong a refusal as the Bible has.

The Potsherd Gate opened toward the valley, perhaps named for the broken pottery thrown out there. Jeremiah brings a whole jar to the place of broken jars.

Verse 9 uses the language of the covenant curses in Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28, which had warned long before where abandoning God would lead. Lamentations records that it happened.
passages.later: Kings tells that Josiah ‘desecrated Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom so that no one could sacrifice his son or daughter in the fire’ (2 Kings 23:10). The law had warned of the siege of verse 9 (Deuteronomy 28:53).
passages.hard:
Verse 9 says God will make people eat their own children in the siege. Does God cause such a horror?

This is one of the most terrible verses in the Bible, and it describes something that really happened in ancient sieges when food ran out (2 Kings 6:28-29; Lamentations 4:10). It speaks in the words of the covenant curses, which warned Israel ahead of time where abandoning God would lead. Most interpreters read God's words as his handing the city over to the siege and what follows, not as God directly willing the act; the Hebrew Bible often speaks of God as the cause of what he permits as judgment. There is also a bitter match in the chapter: a people who burned their children to Baal would see their children lost again.

The verse is not there to be explained away. It shows how terrible the fruit of idolatry and violence becomes, and how seriously God takes the blood of the innocent. No child's suffering is a verdict on the child.

If you carry grief or guilt about a pregnancy, or about the loss of a child before or after birth, please know that you are met with gentleness here, not judgment. God knows your story too. Please talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: God says the killing of children never entered his mind. Ask what the world you live in sacrifices its children to, in pursuit of security or success. And ask what it would mean to take the blood of the innocent as seriously as God does.

passages.happening:
Then Jeremiah is to smash the jar in front of the men with him (verse 10). God will shatter this nation and city ‘like one shatters a potter’s jar that can never again be repaired’ (verse 11). They will bury the dead in Topheth until there is no room (verse 11). God will make the city like Topheth (verse 12). The houses of Jerusalem and of the kings, where people burned incense on the rooftops to the host of heaven, will be defiled like that place (verse 13).

Jeremiah comes back from Topheth, stands in the court of the LORD's house, and tells all the people that God is about to bring on the city and its villages every disaster he has announced, ‘because they have stiffened their necks so as not to heed My words’ (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
In chapter 18 the clay was still soft on the wheel, and the potter could reshape it. Now the jar is fired and hard. Once it is smashed, it cannot be mended. The two chapters belong together: there was a time to be reshaped, and it has passed.

The witnesses were elders and leading priests, the people responsible for the city. They watched the sign with their own eyes.

Rooftops were flat and used for living and for worship. People burned incense there to the sun, moon and stars.

The next chapter tells what happened when Jeremiah repeated this message in the temple: he was beaten and put in the stocks.
passages.later: A psalm uses the same picture of judgment: ‘You will shatter them like pottery’ (Psalm 2:9). Zephaniah condemns ‘those who bow on the rooftops to worship the host of heaven’ (Zephaniah 1:5).
passages.asks: The soft clay could be reshaped; the fired jar could only be broken. Ask whether there is something in your life still soft enough to change. And ask whether you are putting off a turning that will not always be possible.
